main.title: Front Mission 5: Scars of the War
main.subtitle: A soldier grows older inside the conflict
main.summary: Front Mission 5: Scars of the War is Square Enix's PlayStation 2 tactical role-playing game, released in Japan on 29 December 2005. Its campaign follows Walter Feng through a military career shaped by the recurring conflicts of the Front Mission world. Wanzers again carry the fighting, with pilots and interchangeable machinery forming the squad the player prepares before a mission. The title's interest in the marks left by war gives continuity to that structure. The next deployment is another stage in a life rather than an isolated tactical exercise.

cards.heading: A soldier grows older inside the conflict
cards.text: Front Mission 5: Scars of the War is Square Enix's PlayStation 2 tactical role-playing game, released in Japan on 29 December 2005. Its campaign follows Walter Feng through a military career shaped by the recurring conflicts of the Front Mission world. Wanzers again carry the fighting, with pilots and interchangeable machinery forming the squad the player prepares before a mission. The title's interest in the marks left by war gives continuity to that structure. The next deployment is another stage in a life rather than an isolated tactical exercise.

cards.heading: Position several machines for one action
cards.text: Action Points limit what each unit can do, connecting movement and attack to the resources available during a turn. Links allow nearby allies to support an action, making placement useful beyond the range of one weapon. A squad that has been carefully assembled still needs a formation that lets its parts cooperate. Between missions, bases and camps provide time to organise pilots and equipment. The player moves repeatedly between these two kinds of planning: deciding what the unit should carry, then deciding where it should stand when the fighting begins.

cards.heading: The final main PlayStation 2 campaign
cards.text: Shintaro Tamai directed the game, with Toshiro Tsuchida producing and Hidenori Iwasaki composing the score. It gathers mechanics and setting details from across the series into a campaign that looks back over its wars through one soldier's experience. The original release remained Japan-only. An English fan translation appeared in 2009, allowing another audience to follow the story. Within Front Mission, Scars of the War gives the tactical systems a particularly long view, connecting successive battles to the people who survive them and return to serve again.

main.title: Irrational Games
main.subtitle: From a small studio to the Take-Two acquisition
main.summary: On January 9, 2006 Take-Two announces the acquisition of Irrational Games.

cards.heading: Irrational joins Take-Two
cards.text: Take-Two announced its acquisition of Irrational Games on January 9, 2006. Founded by Ken Levine, Jon Chey and Rob Fermier, the studio had developed System Shock 2, Freedom Force and SWAT 4 before joining 2 K. These games used different settings but shared an interest in the choices players could make within them. The acquisition accompanied BioShock's move towards a larger production, bringing the small studio's approach into a new phase of its history.

cards.heading: Three founders in Cambridge
cards.text: Irrational began in 1997 with Ken Levine, Jon Chey and Rob Fermier, drawing on experience close to Looking Glass. Levine later recalled a three-person studio working from a living room in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The team wanted distinctive worlds and characters, with environments that responded to the player's use of tools. That interest connected projects with very different visual styles and settings.

cards.heading: Learning the systems of the Von Braun
cards.text: System Shock 2 places exploration, combat, hacking, character statistics and resource management aboard the Von Braun. Its systems repeatedly draw on the same security cameras, inventory, powers and enemies. The team's postmortem describes working with a limited budget and reusing these elements. A player can approach a problem through different abilities, but each approach consumes resources. That combination makes learning the ship's rules important to survival.

cards.heading: Superheroes, police and a changing catalogue
cards.text: Freedom Force brings superhero comics into squad tactics, while SWAT 4 builds police missions around procedures, commands and the use of believable spaces. These projects gave Irrational experience beyond System Shock's science-fiction setting. Each asked players to learn a set of rules and consider the consequences of an action. Take-Two's 2006 catalogue announcement placed those different games together as the studio joined 2 K.

main.title: Wii
main.subtitle: A familiar gesture opens a door
main.summary: Nintendo made swinging, pointing and sharing the room central to a console's design.

cards.heading: An action explained by a gesture
cards.text: Wii's motion-sensitive remote offered a different invitation from an increasingly complicated gamepad. Its design asked how a wider range of people could understand an action by performing a familiar gesture.

cards.heading: Making room for more players
cards.text: President Satoru Iwata's interviews documented the collaborative decisions behind the machine and its software. The ambition was not only new hardware: it was a broader place for play in everyday family life.

sources.title: Iwata Asks — Wii closing statement, 7 December 2006

cards.heading: A prototype finds its sport
cards.text: Wii Sports began among experiments made to test possible controllers. Tennis director Keizo Ota recalls receiving different hardware proposals and quickly building software around them. The remote's rod-like shape suggested a racket. The process also ran in reverse: a working game gave the hardware team something concrete to examine. Producer Katsuya Eguchi later had to turn these scattered prototypes into a coherent collection. The gesture did not arrive first as a finished instruction for a finished machine. Its usefulness became visible while people tried competing proposals together.

cards.heading: Someone nearby has advice
cards.text: Spectators also became part of the development team's observations. During demonstrations, Takayuki Shimamura noticed people advising the baseball player about their swing, even though conventional sporting form was not required by the controls. Keizo Ota imagined friends and relatives trying Tennis despite rarely playing games. The team began considering whether an action could be understood and discussed by people watching, giving someone nearby a reason to ask for the next turn.

cards.heading: A strap becomes a design problem
cards.text: Moving the controller gave a small physical component new importance. A December 2006 US notice records Nintendo's wrist-strap replacement programme after cords broke when players used excessive force and accidentally released the remote. It reports three minor injuries not requiring medical attention, all during Wii Sports. The affected programme covered about two million straps. The same gesture intended to make play immediately understandable had to coexist with hands, furniture and people nearby. The accessory was part of that interaction, not simply packaging around it.

cards.heading: A small part changes
cards.text: The revised wrist strap used a cord 1.0 millimetre in diameter, replacing the original 0.6-millimetre cord. Nintendo offered replacement straps to consumers, and the notice identified the dates after which new console packages and separate remotes should include the stronger version. This small change addressed the physical use of a controller already present in millions of homes, complementing the software team's work on making a swing feel understandable.

main.title: Dwarf Fortress
main.summary: Dwarf Fortress (previously titled Slaves to Armok: God of Blood Chapter II: Dwarf Fortress) is a construction and management simulation and roguelike indie video game created by Bay 12 Games.

cards.heading: Two developers build an ongoing world
cards.text: Dwarf Fortress (previously titled Slaves to Armok: God of Blood Chapter II: Dwarf Fortress) is a construction and management simulation and roguelike indie video game created by Bay 12 Games. Available as freeware and in development since 2002, its first alpha version was released in 2006 and received attention for being a two-member project surviving solely on donations.

cards.heading: A fortress inside a generated history
cards.text: Originally displayed using ASCII art, the game takes place in a procedurally generated fantasy world with its own creatures, inhabitants and history. Players manage a colony of dwarves in fortress mode or explore the world as an individual adventurer. The simulation links the colony to the larger world, producing stories through the interaction of its many systems.

cards.heading: From Armok to a new graphical edition
cards.text: Prior to Dwarf Fortress, Tarn Adams was working on a project called Slaves to Armok: God of Blood which was a role-playing game. By 2004, Adams decided to shift from the original Armok to Dwarf Fortress after the former became difficult to maintain. Adams calls it his life's work and said in 2011 that version 1.0 will not be ready for at least another 20 years, and even after that he would continue to work on it. A paid edition with graphical tiles and a new soundtrack was published by Kitfox Games and released to Steam and Itch.io in 2022.

cards.heading: Complexity, community and the meaning of failure
cards.text: Critics praised the depth and emergent play while noting the steep learning curve. Dwarf Fortress influenced games including Minecraft and RimWorld, and entered the Museum of Modern Art collection in 2012. Its active community shares accounts of successful settlements and disastrous failures, summed up by the motto: "Losing is Fun!"

main.title: Rule of Rose
main.subtitle: A hierarchy written in red crayon
main.summary: Rule of Rose is Punchline's PlayStation 2 psychological-horror game, first released in Japan on 19 January 2006. Set in Britain in 1930, it follows Jennifer into a world controlled by girls who have organised themselves as the Red Crayon Aristocrats. Their demands and social rules give the adventure an oppressive structure, making humiliation and exclusion part of its fear. Jennifer searches for meaning within this uncertain world with the help of her dog, Brown. The game builds its unease around childhood memories and the power that a group can exercise over somebody outside it.

cards.heading: A hierarchy written in red crayon
cards.text: Rule of Rose is Punchline's PlayStation 2 psychological-horror game, first released in Japan on 19 January 2006. Set in Britain in 1930, it follows Jennifer into a world controlled by girls who have organised themselves as the Red Crayon Aristocrats. Their demands and social rules give the adventure an oppressive structure, making humiliation and exclusion part of its fear. Jennifer searches for meaning within this uncertain world with the help of her dog, Brown. The game builds its unease around childhood memories and the power that a group can exercise over somebody outside it.

cards.heading: Let Brown find what Jennifer cannot
cards.text: Brown can follow the scent of objects, helping Jennifer locate items needed to continue. The partnership gives exploration a practical relationship rather than leaving the dog only as a figure in the story. Finding what the children demand can mean searching spaces that remain difficult to understand, while encounters expose Jennifer's vulnerability. The player gradually assembles connections between objects, places and memories. That process supports the psychological horror: an ordinary possession can acquire a disturbing significance because of the circumstances in which it is requested, found or remembered.

cards.heading: A troubling reputation beyond the game
cards.text: Punchline developed the project after Sony requested a horror game, drawing on fairy tales and an interest in the uncertain world of childhood. Yutaka Minobe's score was performed by studio musicians, giving the atmosphere a deliberately human texture. Rumours about its content caused a moral panic before the European release and contributed to cancellation in the United Kingdom. Reviews were mixed, particularly about the gameplay. The game's later reputation rests more on its story, music and imagery, which leave the player interpreting the cruelty and memories behind Jennifer's experience.

main.title: Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams
main.summary: Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams, released in Japan as Shin Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams, is a 2006 action role-playing game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Soki faces Hideyoshi and the Genma
cards.text: Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams is Capcom's 2006 PlayStation 2 action role-playing game. Set in Japan decades after Onimusha 3: Demon Siege, it follows Soki, a warrior with Oni powers opposing Hideyoshi Toyotomi and the demonic Genma army. Allies join him with the same goal, giving the journey a larger playable cast. It first appeared in Japan in January before North American and European releases in March.

cards.heading: Fighting beside an ally
cards.text: Dawn of Dreams expands the range of attacks and weapons and lets the player fight beside computer-controlled allies. Orders influence their actions, and a button switches direct control between characters. A three-dimensional camera replaces most of the earlier fixed views. Returning to previous stages can reveal new content, although story progression eventually closes access to some areas. The team pursued these expanded action systems after working on Shadow of Rome, responding to demand for another Onimusha.

cards.heading: Reception and later adaptations
cards.text: Following its release, Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams received good critical response, but it generated poor sales. Writers praised the action, graphics, characters, and exploration elements but also criticized some elements from its presentation, including its dialogue, English voice acting, and some of the cutscenes being blurry and low resolution. Dawn of Dreams also received a film adaptation (consisting of in-game footage and cutscenes) and two manga spin-offs. This is also the first Onimusha where the main character is not based on an actor's likeness.

main.title: Chibi-Robo!
main.subtitle: A House Seen from Ten Centimeters
main.summary: Skip turns a suburban house into an adventure for a robot ten centimeters tall, with chores, living toys and a battery that regularly needs charging.

cards.heading: A House Seen from Ten Centimeters
cards.text: Skip developed Chibi-Robo! for Nintendo GameCube, with the North American release arriving on February 6, 2006. The small robot joins the Sanderson household to make its inhabitants happy. Cleaning, carrying objects and helping the family open routes through rooms that look enormous from his height. The power cord trailing behind him is essential: every outing must leave enough battery power to reach an outlet.

cards.heading: An Ordinary House Becomes a Continent
cards.text: A table becomes a platform and the edge of a sink becomes a wall. Each room asks the player to examine furniture, steps and narrow gaps for a route that a ten-centimeter robot can use. Familiar household objects become tools and obstacles as Chibi-Robo moves between the bedrooms, garden and other parts of the house.

cards.heading: Doing Good Consumes Energy
cards.text: The battery drains while Chibi-Robo moves and works. Cleaning stains, collecting rubbish and helping characters earn Happy Points, but the robot must regularly stop at an electrical outlet and plug himself in. Director Kenichi Nishi placed this need at the center of the design: a robot made to help others consumes energy while doing so. Planning the next task also means planning the return journey.

cards.heading: Behind the Chores Is a Family Coming Apart
cards.text: The Sanderson family has problems beyond a dirty floor: the father spends irresponsibly, the mother is exhausted and their daughter speaks like a frog. Toys come alive while the humans are away. Chores introduce Chibi-Robo to these characters and their stories, giving him reasons to revisit each room. Nishi described the adventure as a digital picture book, with small acts of help carrying the story forward.

main.title: Forbidden Siren 2
main.subtitle: An island whose past will not stay buried
main.summary: Forbidden Siren 2 is Sony's PlayStation 2 survival-horror game, first released in Japan on 9 February 2006. Several people become trapped on Yamijima Island, where the population vanished during a blackout decades earlier. A capsized ferry and a crashed military helicopter bring different characters into the same mystery. The story is experienced out of order, letting one person's discoveries change the meaning of another's predicament. Its island becomes a place the player learns through overlapping fragments, while the immediate problem remains finding a way past the hostile figures moving through the dark.

cards.heading: An island whose past will not stay buried
cards.text: Forbidden Siren 2 is Sony's PlayStation 2 survival-horror game, first released in Japan on 9 February 2006. Several people become trapped on Yamijima Island, where the population vanished during a blackout decades earlier. A capsized ferry and a crashed military helicopter bring different characters into the same mystery. The story is experienced out of order, letting one person's discoveries change the meaning of another's predicament. Its island becomes a place the player learns through overlapping fragments, while the immediate problem remains finding a way past the hostile figures moving through the dark.

cards.heading: See the danger from another pair of eyes
cards.text: Sightjacking allows the player to look through the perceptions of other characters and enemies, gathering information that the protagonist cannot safely obtain in person. That borrowed view can reveal a patrol's position or a route that might otherwise be approached blindly. Missions ask for specific objectives, often involving escape, an item or an enemy that must be dealt with. The Link Navigator organises the scenarios and their relationships. An action in one part of the story can make another objective possible elsewhere, turning the chronology into part of the puzzle.

cards.heading: Another strand of Sony's horror games
cards.text: Keiichiro Toyama directed the sequel, with Naoko Sato contributing to the writing and Kuniaki Haishima composing its music. The cast's intersecting stories and unusual ways of seeing continue the first Siren's approach to survival horror. Japanese, Australian and European releases arrived in 2006, but the game did not receive a North American edition. Its fear grows from imperfect information: the player can borrow another viewpoint without gaining complete control of the situation. Understanding what an enemy sees is useful precisely because being seen by that enemy can be disastrous.

main.title: Suikoden V
main.subtitle: A prince gathers a country around him
main.summary: Suikoden V is a PlayStation 2 role-playing game developed by Konami and Hudson Soft, first released in Japan on 23 February 2006. The Prince of Falena becomes caught in the political struggles of his homeland, travelling to gather allies as the conflict develops. Set before the first Suikoden, it returns the series to a story where a large cast gives a national crisis a personal scale. Recruitment is part of the journey rather than an activity separated from it. Every new companion can make the prince's cause more than a claim inherited at court.

cards.heading: A prince gathers a country around him
cards.text: Suikoden V is a PlayStation 2 role-playing game developed by Konami and Hudson Soft, first released in Japan on 23 February 2006. The Prince of Falena becomes caught in the political struggles of his homeland, travelling to gather allies as the conflict develops. Set before the first Suikoden, it returns the series to a story where a large cast gives a national crisis a personal scale. Recruitment is part of the journey rather than an activity separated from it. Every new companion can make the prince's cause more than a claim inherited at court.

cards.heading: A useful ally may require a small detour
cards.text: New recruits often have their own conditions or short quests, encouraging the player to investigate people and places beyond the next main objective. Towns provide information, equipment and opportunities to improve weapons or learn skills. More than sixty characters can take part in combat, while others support the group in different ways. The growing community therefore has uses beyond filling a roster. A return visit may reveal somebody who can now be persuaded to join, connecting the player's attention to the world with the strength of the alliance being built.

cards.heading: Return to the series' wider political story
cards.text: Takahiro Sakiyama directed the game, with Kazuyoshi Tsugawa writing its account of Falena's competing interests. The viewpoint and party structure recall aspects of the earlier Suikoden games while using three-dimensional environments and characters. Released internationally during 2006, it became the final main numbered entry in the original series. Its appeal rests on the connection between individual recruitment and larger events. The prince's travels are not only a route through the plot: they are the means by which a divided country gradually acquires a group capable of changing its direction.

main.title: FIFA Street 2
main.summary: FIFA Street 2 expands EA's four-a-side football game with new tricks, career progression and an in-game radio station.

cards.heading: A new trick stick for street football
cards.text: FIFA Street 2 is EA's 2006 follow-up to FIFA Street. It introduces a new trick-stick system and a larger range of football tricks. GameCube, PlayStation 2 and Xbox versions were accompanied by handheld and mobile editions. Portugal international Cristiano Ronaldo appears on the cover.

cards.heading: Different results on home consoles and handhelds
cards.text: Reviews of the home-console editions noted improvements over the first FIFA Street while remaining mixed overall. The handheld versions were less well received, particularly on Nintendo DS, where critics felt several of those additions were missing. The platform therefore made a substantial difference to the sequel's reception.

cards.heading: Building a team in Rule the Streets
cards.text: The game is a street soccer game in which the player can take control of 4-a-side versions of national football teams in matches where the object is to win by scoring a set number of goals or points via tricks, or within a time limit. In the career mode "Rule the Streets", one creates a player and competes in tournaments around the world to obtain "Skill Bills" to buy clothing and upgrade his rating. As the player improves, he can captain his own street soccer team and eventually become an international. The best players have special moves often named after their nickname.

cards.heading: Zane Lowe presents the radio
cards.text: The game has its own in-game radio station, presented by Zane Lowe formerly of BBC Radio 1 and featuring music by artists such as Roots Manuva, Sway, Pendulum, Editors and The Subways.

cards.heading: A mixed critical reception
cards.text: The game received "mixed" reviews on all platforms except the DS version, which received "unfavorable" reviews, according to video game review aggregator Metacritic.

cards.heading: The difficulty of defending against tricks
cards.text: Reviewers singled out defending as a weakness. The A.V. Club described the difficulty of reacting to tricks as a source of accidental comedy, while The Times felt defending let down the PlayStation 2 and Xbox versions. These criticisms sat alongside the appeal of performing moves and building a team in the career.
